speechtext:
I do not think the question
requires any answer. The intentions of the government are not made manifest by question and answer.
Notwithstanding this I thought perhaps the Prime Minister could indicate to the house the intention of the government.

Hon. ROBERT WEIR (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the house go into committee on Bill No. 26, respecting fruit.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

I understand the minister desires to have a slight amendment made to clause 1. It is just a slight amendment to the title. I move:
That section 1 be amended to read: "This act may be cited as the Fruit and Honey Act, 1934."
The amendment is to include the words "and honey" in the title of the bill.
Amendment agreed to.
May I ask the minister why the home consumption of honey in 1932-33 as compared with 1930-31 has decreased by 9,535,000 pounds, and whether this legislation will remedy that?
That will have to wait to be demonstrated.
May I ask the minister also why the home consumption of apples in 1932-33 as compared with 1930-31 has decreased by 1,209,000 barrels?

Without accepting as authoritative the figures given by the hon. member, I may say that the situation is this, not necessarily that there is less production, but that there has been a greater export which might account, if his figures' are correct, for the smaller domestic consumption.

Then the minister should have resort to the old adage: "An apple a day keeps the doctor away." I notice from the explanation given by the minister, in the last year for which statistics are available, the home consumption of apples and honey has decreased considerably on account of the fact that our people have no money with which to buy those articles. I ask the minister to be kind enough to table a report showing the exports, the imports, the production and the home consumption of the fruit, also of honey, mentioned in the speech made by the right hon. Prime Minister on October 12, 1932, in which the right hon. gentleman told the house of his expectations in connection with imperial trade in relation to fruit.

What are the figures for home consumption?
The home consumption I take it would be the difference between production and export.
Are there no imports?
And with the imports taken into consideration, yes.
What was the average price each year?
The records I have here are not complete in that respect. I shall be glad to let the hon. member have this information at the earliest possible time next week.
Will the hon. gentleman admit that the figure I have already given is correct?
I could not say without checking it up.
Would the minister be kind enough to tell us about dried apples, the production in each year since 1930, the exports, the home consumption, and the imports?

I shall be glad to give this information at a later time in connection with the estimates on fruit. We have not got all the information here. I do not know whether this is the proper time to prolong a discussion on the request for such information, but I shall be glad to give the information when the estimates are up.

I thank the hon. gentleman. But we have before us now a bill of importance which is supposed to assist the farmer in the sale of his fruit and honey. There is a large decrease in the home consumption of apples and of honey, therefore we must have that information before discussing the bill. If we take the estimates and pass them in the meantime we shall have to do it with our eyes shut. Therefore I ask the hon. minister if it is not possible for him to give that information right now, as he has the fruit commissioner of his department before him.
Shall the item carry?

No, Mr. Chairman, I
would like the hon. gentleman to answer my question.
I regret I was not able to hear the hon. member's question. If he would repeat it and it is possible for me to hear it-

I shall repeat it as many
times as the minister wishes.

Order; may I ask the committee to
keep better order? It is very difficult to hear.

I .thank you very much,
sir, for the dignity with which you conduct the committee. I shall put it another way.
1	shall ask the minister to tell us what kind of fruit will be sold in greater quantity on account of this legislation, or what are the fruits the sale of which might be affected by this bill?

No person could
answer that question, I believe. This is in great part a revision of an act that has been in force for thirty-three years. It has been submitted to the committee on agriculture and colonization, they have gone into it very fully and have adopted it without amendment.

It becomes important to
see the definition of fruit as given in section
2	of this bill, because the act is to be known as the Fruit Act, 1934. The first thing we have to know is what kinds of fruit are affected by the bill. It is said that:
"fruit" means fruit of every kind grown in Canada, known botanically as such, except wild fruit in respect of which no grades are prescribed.
I understand quite well that this bill has nothing to do with wild strawberries, raspberries, blueberries and so on, because they are considered as wild fruit, except some special kinds of strawberries and raspberries which grow in gardens and greenhouses. At this time of year I do not speak about wild strawberries. But there are greenhouse strawberries and cultivated raspberries which might be affected by this bill. Also I understand that this bill has nothing to do with bananas and pineapples that do not grow in Canada. Fruit means fruit of every kind grown in Canada; therefore we will leave aside the blueberries which grow wild. I wonder if the hon. gentleman is ready to accept that contention, that blueberries are not included under the word "fruit" in this bill. The same question would apply to cranberries.

Cranberries are not included, and will not be included unless a special request is made by the provinces to have this done. Quebec has already made such request in regard to blueberries, and the word " fruit " will be interpreted to include that fruit.

Thank you. Now let us
be very particular. We have peaches, pears,

Fruit and Honey Act
plums and gooseberries; we have mentioned apples. Here we have four or five kinds of fruit largely grown in Canada. Would the minister be kind enough to give us some information as to the production, consumption, importation and exportation of these fruits? We have had some information already with regard to apples; could we have the same information with regard to plums, peaches, pears and gooseberries?

We have not that
information with us. We did not think these questions would be asked except on the estimates, but I will be glad to get the information for the hon. gentleman.

I regret very much that
the minister takes that stand. We are willing to support him if he proves to us that this bill will be of some benefit to the fruit growers. Some hon. gentleman mentioned cherries, another delicious, Canadian-grown fruit, and there are also other fruits I have not mentioned. I am sorry the minister takes that stand, because that means we will have no information before this bill is reported by the committee, and this is where we must ask the minister for that information. When it was stated that this bill would come up today I was sure the minister would be fully prepared to answer questions of this kind, which are closely related to the bill. The estimates do not come up until later; we take only one step at a time. This is the first step; this is the act, the law of the country regarding fruit and fruit growers, and it is of the utmost importance because of some competition which arises early in the spring through imports from the United States and other countries. I believe the minister is too fair to insist upon putting this bill through the committee before the information asked for is made available to every member of the committee. Does the minister insist on his stand or will he reconsider his position.

I shall be glad to
supply any information asked for by the hon. member.

I wonder if the minister
could tell me how this bill compares with the bill that was considered by the Ontario fruit growers' convention?

The draft of this bill has been submitted to the various provincial fruit conventions held throughout Canada during the past six months. The Norfolk county fruit growers, communicated with the department concerning the bill. I can say that it has been approved by all provincial fruit growers' conventions throughout Canada, before which it has been placed during the past six months.
It is practically in the form approved by the Ontario growers?
Yes.

I should like to direct the attention of the committee to the fact that we are still on section 1, the short title. I think it would be better to pass this section and get on to section 2. The discussion is wandering very far afield from section 1, which has only to do with the title.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, and in that connection I would point out that the bill has been very carelessly drafted. Honey is mentioned in part 3 and in other places as well; therefore the title should have been drafted accordingly.
The title has been amended.

I do not mean to say that the amendment is wrong; I believe the amendment is very proper, but the bill should have been properly drafted and the title should have appeared as it is now suggested by the amendment.

I believe I am in order in addressing these remarks to the minister at this time. May I say that the success of this act, which in its present form is wide open with regard to the specifications of fruit containers and so on, will depend entirely upon the way it is administered by the department. In that connection I should like to direct attention to the fact that on March 7 I asked for certain information in connection with the inspection of fruits and vegetables in the different provinces of Canada. The answers I received contained no information at all, and in my opinion were a straight attempt on the part of somebody to evade the necessity of giving proper answers. On February 15 I asked for the same information, and the answers I received then were erroneous, in my opinion; I believe the minister has acknowledged that they were not correct.
I am simply bringing up this matter at the present time to show that without the full cooperation of the fruit branch with the fruit growers under this act, the interests of the fruit growers will not be properly looked after. I should like to go further and place on Hansard a letter which I received from the Minister of Agriculture under date of March

12. From the standpoint of the fruit growers in my riding this was the only way in which they could get the answers to the questions I had asked. Under date of March 12, the Minister of Agriculture wrote me as follows, in regard to the question to which I have referred:

Clause (d) of subsection 3 reads:
To provide for the inspection, certification and grading of any kind of fruit and the inspection fees which shall be payable.

In regard to this clause of the bill I should like to ask the minister if it is the intention, under the bill, to continue the charge for inspection fees on apples in car lots?

I would suggest
that the discussion be confined to the section now before the committee. The hon. member who has just spoken has directed his remarks to a clause which appears later in the bill. I believe we would make better progress by taking each section as we come to it. However now that the remarks of the hon. member will appear in Hansard I should like to make a few observations in regard to the statements he has made. In the first place, the questions as placed on the order paper by the hon. member were not interpreted by the officials to mean what he evidently had in mind. An hon. member on this side of the house who is interested in this matter stated to me that he did not think the information had been given which the hon. member wanted, or that the officials had riot interpreted the questions as would have been expected by the hon. member. I immediately got in touch with and discussed the matter with him, explaining matters as I felt they should be explained.
The hon. member has left the inference that there must have been some reason for this misinterpretation. I suggest that the best test of that is that I believe he now has the information he required, and I leave it to him or to any other hon. member in the house as to whether or not there is anything in that information which any of the officers in the fruit branch would have tried in anyway to keep from him. I believe the hon. member will agree with me that there is nothing in it which the officials would have tried to keep from him in the first place. There are likely to be different interpretations. In the anxiety of the department to get the information and have it forwarded as soon as possible in this instance they may not, perhaps, have given the matter fhe thought it should have had. I contend, however, that there is nothing in the information which has been supplied which the officers of the department could have desired for any reason to withhold.
With reference to the charges for inspection I would suggest that the questions asked by the hon. member should be left until we reach that part of the bill. Although conditions may change I may say that it is the intention at the present time that charges will be made. I believe there have been no requests from the fruit growers' associations that they should be done away with.

Fruit and Honey Act

I sincerely hope the minister did not misinterpret my statements in connection with these questions, inasmuch as he feels that I was of the opinion there was any particular reason for withholding information, I did not insinuate that. But if anybody will read the question, particularly those officials in charge of the fruit branch who understand not only the phraseology but the practical application and result of the questions, and tell me that the official, whoever he was, did not know what information I required, I would say that the minister should check up on his officials and deliver a copy of Webster's dictionary to them. They understood the questions perfectly well, and they knew what I wanted.
Let me go further: The third section of my question asked on March 7 is as follows:
How many inspection reports upon apples were issued free of charge during the fiscal year ended March 31, 1933?
And the answer was "570," meaning 570 reports. Can the minister tell me why those reports were issued free.

In the case of
violations of the act there is no charge made.

May I
ask a question in connection with the inspection fee on apples under this Fruit Act, which will of course be left to the discretion of the minister and the department? Would it be the policy of the department to continue charging fruit growers an inspection fee for compulsory inspection, or is it the intention of the government to make that fee cover other horticultural and agricultural products as well? I may say to the minister that the fruit growers in my section of the country and throughout the province, with the majority of whom I come in contact, have felt and do feel that they have been and are being penalized in connection with the charge for compulsory inspection of apples. They do not feel that they are being treated in the same manner as are other producers who do not have to pay an inspection fee. It is my information, and I feel I am voicing the sentiments of the apple industry of Ontario, when I say that the department, particularly when the inspection is compulsory, should either indicate a nominal charge or eliminate the inspection charge altogether, and place the fruit growers on the same basis as the honey producers, or some other producers. Hon. members know perfectly well, as do the officers in the Department of Agriculture, that in the last few years the apple growers have had plenty with which to contend, without being penalized, as they feel they have been, by an inspection fee for compulsory inspection.

These charges have been made, so I am advised, at the request of the industry itself. When there is any sufficient representation made objecting to the charge such representation will be given full consideration.

I appreciate the minister's reply as it concerns associations of fruit growers. I have followed the proceedings during the last few months of the committee of the apple growers' associations in the province of Ontario, and if it is the minister's impression that the apple growers of Ontario, and I might enlarge that territory to take in British Columbia and Nova iScotia, are satisfied with the inspection fee, particularly when other products are not penalized to the same extent, I am afraid his impression is entirely erroneous. I would like the minister to assure the committee that consideration will be given to eliminating the fee or that it will be used to advance the interests of the fruit growers throughout the dominion.
I have already stated that consideration will be given.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would again direct
attention to the fact that under section 1, the short title, the discussion has wandered very far afield. It appears to me that it would be much more orderly to pass this section and then proceed with the other sections.

We can
discuss the whole principle on the title, Mr. Chairman.

My understanding of the
rules, Mr. Chairman, is that the principle of the bill can be discussed on the short title. There are a few questions I would like to ask on the principle of the bill. Some of us who have to attend the many special committees of this house have to take such opportunity as presents itself for asking questions on measures in which we are particularly interested.
The first question is, was this bill in its present form presented to the Nova Scotia Fruit Growers' Association, and was it approved in its present form by that body?
My second question is, what situation was the act drafted to meet? What particular abuses is it designed to remedy? What particular change in principle is there between the Fruit Act presently existing and the act as sought to be amended?
If I may be permitted to put all my questions at once, although they are somewhat un-
Fruit and Honey Act

related, my third question is in reference to the fees for fruit inspection. Is it correct, as intimated by my colleague from Northumberland (Mr. Fraser), that apples are the only agricultural commodity for which the producer is charged an inspection fee? If that is correct, then I submit as my colleague from Northumberland has so forcibly done, that that situation should be remedied. The minister has said that no representations have been made by the industry itself to the effect that inspection fees should not be charged, but I am confident that in the province of Nova Scotia there is the impression that we are being treated as regards apples as are the producers of other commodities, and if the fruit growers of the province of Nova Scotia felt that the producers of other agricultural commodities were receiving their inspection at government expense, wthile the producers of apples are having their apples inspected at their own expense, the minister would be overwhelmed with protests in a very short time. As the member for a constituency which is vitally interested in the production and exportation of fruit. I should like the minister to answer these questions.

This bill in practically its present form was presented to the fruit growers of Nova Scotia, and I believe that a copy was also mailed to every member whose name was submitted to the department. There have been one or two minor changes in the bill since, but they are quite minor, and they have been endorsed by the Canadian Horticultural Council at a meeting here with representatives of the fruit industry from, I believe, each province.
In the main this is a revision of the Fruit Act which has been in force for some thirty years, in order to bring it more into line with modern practices in the industry. Apples are not the only commodity which pays a fee for inspection. Within the last two years, at least, the vegetable growers, the turnip growers of Ontario, specially requested that they be allowed to have their vegetables inspected. Vegetables are inspected as well as apples. It is also true that an inspection fee is charged for seed grain inspection. The hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Bouchard) reminds me that there is also an inspection fee charged the wool growers. There is also a fee charged for potato inspection and grape inspection. Personally I think the sound thing would be to have each industry pay for its own inspection. That leaves the industry in an advantageous position to ask for any extension or improvement of the inspection. I

agree that if it is sound for one industry, it should bo the same for all.

The minister's answer is satisfactory so far as it goes, but, on the vital matter of the principle of the bill he has scarcely answered my question. He said the bill was being passed to meet the practices in the industry as they exist to-day. My impression of the bill was that its main object was to eliminate rigidity of regulation. I understand that various matters which before were dealt with by legislation are now to be dealt with by regulation and that the minister has power to alter the regulations from time to time, maybe from day to day, as he may see fit. Is that the essential and central principle of the bill?

I regret, Mr. Chairman, if I omitted answering certain parts of the questions asked by my hon. friend. I would suggest that if one question were asked at a time it might facilitate the work of the committee.
I was simply trying to shorten it.

Power is being given to the minister to make regulations where it is felt by the producers as a whole that there should be greater flexibility to deal with situations that arise, such a situation, for instance, as arose in Nova Scotia two years ago, when the second last crop of apples suffered in a big windstorm which knocked down much of the fruit. I stated when this bill was introduced that as long as I held this position, regulations or any changes in them would be submitted to the industry for its approval.
Another change in principle, and this has been almost universally requested, is that brokers, commission agents and dealers, should be licensed and bonded for the protection of the producers.
Another change, perhaps not altogether in the principle, but to a certain extent it is because it comes under the heading of grading, is that fruit that is not fit for consumption cannot be offered for sale except to cider mills or otherwise where it will not come directly into human consumption without being processed.

Would the minister tell the committee whether there is any other agricultural commodity the inspection of which is compulsory, as in the case of apples for export, where the producer is compelled to pay the cost of the inspection, and if so what?

Fruit and Honey Act

Can the minister give the
list of commodities inspected by the government free to the producer?

I cannot offhand,
but I shall be glad to submit that information.

That constitutes the great
bulk of agricultural commodities.

No the grain growers pay for the inspection of their grain by a levy, and grain is a very large item, perhaps the largest single item in agricultural products in the export trade. Seeds and hay also pay for their own inspection.

In discussing the principle of this measure the minister made a reference a few minutes ago, when explaining how the bill was drafted, to the Canadian Horticultural Council. Does the minister consider the Canadian Horticultural Council a representative instrument of the fruit growers?

I should say, from
the information available to myself, yes. I know personally a number of those who are members of the Canadian Horticultural Council and my understanding is that they are active apple producers and fruit farmers.

I am
very glad to have that reply from the minister because my information, from my dealings and association with the fruit growers and the officials of the Canadian Horticultural Council, is exactly the same as the minister's. I would therefore ask the minister, in view of the fact that this is practically a wide open act so far as specifications and grades are concerned, whether the regulations and changes involved in the sections of the bill will be submitted to the Canadian Horticultural Council, and whether the fruit branch will be guided by the advice of that body.

The regulations will be submitted to the Canadian Horticultural Council as well as to any other representative
fruit growers' association in the dominion, and the branch will no doubt be guided by their recommendations.

Referring again to the official body known as the Canadian Horticultural Council, representing the fruit and vegetable growers, and affiliated industries, I would ask the minister this question. When considering the continued application of the inspection fee, which I take it from the minister's remarks is the intention of his department, will he take into consideration the advisability, if that fee is levied for these inspection charges, of contributing at least a part of the fee to the Canadian Horticultural Council or to any other established or acknowledged representative body of fruit growers, to assist their work in the interests of the fruit growers?
I have already stated that any representations made with reference to the charge of a fee wil be given every consideration.

With

I think that the hon. members who have taken exception to the phraseology of clause 4 can rest assured that the officials of the fruit branch in conjunction with the industry and the consuming public have only one objective, and that is to regulate the handling of fruit in Canada in the interests of the three branches of the industry and the consuming public. Like my hon. friend from Melville I am quite prepared to support this bill in its present form, having confidence in the officials of the fruit branch and knowing their conscientious anxiety to help the industry in every possible way. That has been our experience-I am speaking of the fruit growers-with the fruit branch. I have no doubt that this act as presented to this committee will be administered by the fruit branch to the satisfaction of everybody just as they have performed their administrative duties in the past. The only fear in my mind has been the point I have brought up. They may under certain conditions, owing to recommendations that have been made by fruit associations in different parts of the country, feel it is necessaiy for them to put into force

regulations under this bill either too soon or too late to suit the conditions of the industry. If the hon. member for Melville and the hon. member for Northumberland are going to desert me perhaps I had better withdraw my amendment. If they prefer to deal in trust and hope and faith and charity as compared with the strict letter of the law, that is their privilege. For my part, a long experience has taught me to fear God and trust no man, and I much prefer to see what I want put in the act, rather than trusting to the good judgment and fair-mindedness of somebody else. There is this difference, that you have to wait for another amending act of parliament to change the act if changes are found desirable and that would take a year probably to do, while frequently you want changes in mid-season to suit the vagaries of the weather and changes in the type and quality of the fruit. Regulations therefore can be changed at any time of the year, and that is why they are much more serviceable to those whom we are trying to serve, mainly the consumers and the producers.

In no case should a copy of the Fruit Act be sent out to an applicant who requests it unless a copy of the regulations is nailed right on to the act as a part of it. Fruit and Honey Act
On section 14-carelessly destroying fruit, etc.

I call the attention of the minister to this section:
Every person who carelessly handles, destroys or pilfers any fruit in the process of packing or handling in transportation, warehousing or otherwise, shall be guilty of an offence.
The penalty used to be not more than $25, but now, under section 20, it is provided that the penalty for a first offence shall be a fine not exceeding $50 and not less than $25. That is too drastic for any very trivial offence. This is not a matter of fraud or the misrepresentation of grade, or trying to put anything over the public; the offence might consist merely in careless handling. Who has not carelessly handled fruit? A man may get a contract to truck fruit to be taken twenty-five miles away and while loading it, a pretty girl comes round the corner and his attention is momentarily diverted; one of the boxes falls and a corner is broken. The man has no opportunity to evade punishment even for a first offence and the minimum fine is not less than $25. I suggest that this is out of keeping with the penalty imposed for any ordinary offence such as careless handling. I believe it is the experience in all criminal jurisprudence that severe penalties do not lead to the enforcement of law but rather to the evasion of it, because the magistrate, who is generally a decent man, will not impose a heavy penalty as a minimum, and rather than do that he will let the defendant off. Moderate penalties should be resorted to. I will not put the point to a vote, but I would ask the minister why he thinks it necessary to double the penalty that was formerly imposed.

This was one point on which there was no difference of opinion in the recommendations of any of the associations. They were all of one mind, that because of the lightness of the penalty as it existed it was not a sufficient deterrent to offences.

The minister is aware of the discussion which has already taken place with regard to the action of the board of pension commissioners in making deductions from or completely suspending pensions of pensioners in cases in which it was considered there had been some irregularity as to marriages, or where proof of marriage had not been sufficiently established. speakeroldname: Hon. MURRAY MacLAREN (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The reviews as carried on by the pension commission began on or about February 1, 1933. The amended Pension Act did not become operative until October 1. 1933. During that interval while the amendments to the act were not operative reviews were held regarding a considerable number of cases, without the application of the principles which were laid down in the amended act. That is to say, the cases concerned were not considered before quorums of the pension commission, and decisions were reached in those cases a,s a result of inquiries and completion of forms submitted to the men concerned. As a result, in some cases pensions were either cancelled or reduced. Had the amended Pension Act then been operative the procedure would have been different. It was laid down in the act that before these cases are considered the people interested shall have an opportunity of appearing before a quorum, and be given a hearing. Following that, decisions may be reached.

Does
that section of last year's legislation apply to the marriage cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I understand that it does. It is true that the hearings are held on the ground of basis of entitlement.
That was an omission made in last year's legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
As these cases were then dealt with in a manner different from that which would have been followed had the act

Supply-Pensions-European War
been operative, and in a way which parliament had intended should be followed when the act became operative, it was felt that in conformity with the general principle of, shall I say, British justice, those who came under the present amendment, whether or not the act was actually operative, should have an opportunity to be heard. As the house is aware, that policy has been followed. As was announced in the house by the Prime Minister, the present position is that those cases which were dealt with between February 1 and October 1, 1933, should be restored to their former status, that such reductions, or amounts arising from such reductions or cancellations should be restored to all those whose hearings before quorums are pending. I understand that very largely the refunding has taken place. A considerable number of cheques were to be made out, and they have all been, or soon will be, refunded.
As to marriage cases I have this to say: There is a good deal of difficulty reaching decisions in such cases and the course which has been followed has been that they are referred to the Department of Justice. I do not know that all such cases have been forwarded, but I do know that either that has been done or they are being prepared for forwarding to that department. I do not know what the advice of the Department of Justice will be, but the pension commission will be advised. I understand that these irregular marriage cases may be classified in certain groups, and that decisions will be reached in accordance with the conditions formed in the different classifications. I have no definite information on that point. So far as I am aware the Department of Justice has not yet advised the pension commission in this connection. If there is any other point about which the hon. member would like to ask, I would be pleased to answer.

The matter to which the minister first referred is not the particular classification I had in mind. However since he has opened the discussion we may as well deal with that angle of the matter. In section 5 of the act passed last year provision was made that pensions should not be cancelled or, due to a change in the basis of entitlement, before the pensioner was afforded an opportunity of appearing before a quorum of the commission. On that point I complain and complain very bitterly that notwithstanding the fact that that was in the act, simply because of the fact that the act was not proclaimed until October 1 the board of pension commissioners proceeded to review nearly 77,000 cases and cancelled or reduced many of them on the ground of a change in the basis of entitlement without any hearing of any kind. That complaint remains, notwithstanding the remedial measures which have been taken. That, it is true, was not in defiance of any act which was in force, but it is in defiance of the spirit of the legislation. I feel quite satisfied that the minister concurs in the idea which parliament had at that time, and that was from the time that this act was passed parliament accepted the principle that a change should not be made in pensions where the basis of entitlement was concerned without giving the man a hearing. The minister concurs, I think, in that principle. It was at least contrary to the spirit of the act that such a change should be made. That is one class of cases to which the minister has referred, but I am not dealing with that class at the moment. I understand from the minister that these pensions where a reduction or cancellation was made on the basis of a change of entitlement have been restored. Is that correct?
Mr. MacLARElN: Yes.
To the full extent which existed before the review was made?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: So I understand. They have been either restored or are in the process of restoration. I think they have been restored, but there were a good many to deal with, and restoration proceeded at once after having been announced in the house. I would like to make this clear, without reflecting on the board of pension commissioners at all, that my view, as a non-legal man, is and has been that it was simply an act of justice that every man, whether in the end he was proved to be in error or not, should have the opportunity of having his case presented and being heard. That is the principle that is pursued in all our courts, that a man has the opportunity of being heard however clear apparently the case against him may be. That is a primary requisite. That has been my view and I am pleased to say that it is the course that is being followed to-day. It is an essential of justice that a man should have the opportunity of a hearing before his case is decided.
I understand that the minister made known his views in that respect to the board of pension commissioners, did he not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Before the minister

The figures submitted to my department are greatly in excess of that number. My information is that there are between 550 and 600 of these cases; I think the department has already received more than 200 files as a first instalment.
I fully realize the difficulty which has been so well stated by my hon. friend from Shel-burne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), and at the present time I cannot see what advantage is

going to result from a reference to the Department of Justice in regard to these cases. At the present moment, through special assistance which we have had to secure, the department is endeavouring to arrange these various cases into categories. I think they will probably fall within seven or eight different categories. There are some cases which I have read over rather hastily which at once present certain difficulties with which we shall be confronted in the majority of these cases. Let me cite one case from British Columbia, where before the war a man and wife were legally married and living together. The woman left her husband, went to Seattle, in the United States, and obtained a divorce from the United States courts. The husband had no domicile in the United States. That divorce was not valid or legal in the Dominion of Canada, but after a few years, just before the war, the husband married again. He thought he had a legal right to marry. He went to the war and became entitled to pension and now, after his death, the question arises as to whether or not he was legally married and whether his children are lawful children or bastards. In my own experience I can recall many marriages, not in military but in civil life, under practically the same circumstances. In all the cases I can recall, not only in Toronto but in Hamilton and Guelph as well, people who have remarried under such conditions have always been considered by their friends in the community as being legally married. Technically I suppose they are not legally married, and if the Department of Justice, on looking into such a case, were bound to give a strict legal opinion, I am afraid we would have to say that the marriage was not valid, or at least that the validity of the marriage was extremely questionable. And if we referred such a case to the court I fear we would secure a decision against the strict validity of the marriage. Both in this country and in Great Britain there is a very strong legal presumption ^ in favour of the validity of marriage; I think perhaps it is one of the strongest of all legal presumptions, and can only be rebutted by positive evidence. Without committing anyone but myself to the views which I now express, I believe that where people have been living together as man and wife the presumption of legal marriage should be allowed to prevail unless there is _ positive testimony to rebut such a presumption.
Let me cite another case which is of some interest, a case where the parties were married in Canada but subsequently removed to the

In the courts of New York, the wife sued for and obtained a divorce, but in the decree of the New York courts a condition was imposed upon the husband forbidding him to remarry. The husband came back to Canada, took up his residence again in Canada, and after the lapse of a few years remarried in this country. There is a very strong legal opinion that the condition imposed by the courts of New York had no validity in this country and consequently that his marriage in this country was valid; and so I would hold. But I believe the board of pension commissioners have taken a different view of the husband's second marriage. I could relate from the cases I have so far read many very peculiar circumstances, but in each case which I have read the parties have been living together as man and wife, and have been assumed by the whole community in which they resided to have been legally married. In such circumstances there is a very strong presumption in favour of a legal marriage, and as I said before unless that presumption can be overcome by positive evidence, the marriage should be held to be legal in all respects. I do not see any way of getting around the difficulty without some further amendment to the act. In the meantime the Department of Justice is endeavouring to separate these marriage cases into various categories. But when this has been done and we are ready to submit the cases for the adjudication of the courts if judgment is to be given on strict legal principles, I am satisfied in a great number of cases the courts will pronounce the marriage to be invalid, just as the board of pension commissioners has done. It is worthy of note, however, that as late as February 26, thirteen days after the announcement was made by the Prime Minister, the chairman of the Canadian pension commission was going blithely on as he had been doing since January, 1933, giving statements to the minister in preparation for this bluebook showing the men who had been cut off the list, and as late as February 26 we have four statements wherein the reason given is "legality of marriage not established." I protest, Mr. Chairman, and will do so more vigorously when we come to consider the personnel of the Canadian pension commission, but I say quite frankly here and now that if the chairman of the Canadian pension commission is not prepared to follow the will of

parliament as submitted through the members representing the various constituencies and passed on through the Minister of Pensions, who is responsible to the country, then the sooner the minister sees that that gentleman is removed the better it will be for this country as a whole.

I would like to say a word or two along a certain line that I have not yet heard touched upon concerning what seems to me the crucial point in the case of these married people who had pensions cut off, and that is that evidence was given sufficient to satisfy the board of pension commissioners in many cases many years ago that the marriage was legal. I have a case, and I think nearly every member of parliament has one or more similar cases from his own neighbourhood, in which the point at issue was this: The couple were married in 1919. The husband and his wife considered that they had proof that the former husband of the woman had died. They were married and their certificate of marriage was accepted by the old board of pension commissioners as proof positive. Now if the board at that time had raised the question of the legality of the marriage it seems to me that a number of these difficulties would have been solved at that time and would not now be arising. In the case I speak of a form was sent out last year asking for the death certificate of the wife's former husband. The parties endeavoured to get that and found out that the man had not been dead at the time they married, as they thought he was. He did not die until 1929. The case again came before the commission; the pension was withheld, and recovery commenced. In this particular case these people remarried immediately to regularize the thing. But if the old board had asked for the death certificate in the first place the case would never have come up. These people could have been legally married in 1929 and the wife would then have been entitled to her allowance, but having gone beyond the first of May of this year they are not legally entitled to it. I wish to congratulate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) on the stand he has taken with regard to the legal position in respect to these cases, and I should also like to put on Hansard a memorandum that was submitted
by the present president of the Canadian legion, a judge of one of our courts in Saskatchewan, in reference to these cases:
It is a well recognized principle of English law that when a marriage is alleged and it is proved that the parties went through a form of marriage and thereafter lived together as man and wife and were by general repute regarded as man and wife this constitutes not an irrebuttable presumption but a presumption rebuttable only by the most conclusive evidence of the validity of marriage.
In the case of Morris vs. Davies, 7 English Reports, page 365, Lord Lindhurst, at page 404, speaking of this presumption said, "that presumption of law is not lightly to be repelled, it is not to be broken in upon or shaken by a mere balance of probability, the: evidence for the purpose of repelling it must be strong, distinct, satisfactory and conclusive." Then in a leading case on the subject, Piers vs. Piers, 9 English Reports, page 1118, the Lord Chancellor, page 1129, expressly approved of the law as stated by Lord Lindhurst. There the fact of the ceremony was not in doubt but no evidence was available to prove that the special licence required by law and necessary to the validity of the marriage had been secured, nevertheless the House of Lords held that the onus was upon the parties seeking to attack the validity of the marriage and upheld the rights of the parties claiming thereunder. To the same effect is the judgment of the privy council in the case of Aronegary Vaigalie, 6 A.C., 364. Once this presumption arises the onus is upon those who seek to attack the validity of the marriage. Goodman vs. Goodman, 28 L.J. ch. 745; Haviland vs. Mortiboy, 32 L.T.O.S., 343; Harrod vs. Harrod, 69 English Reports, 344; Homanuke vs. Homanuke, 13 Saskatchewan L.R. 186, and Hedge vs. Morrow, 20 D.L.R., 561.
This by no means exhausts the law on the subject but it is sufficient to show that the commission are proceeding upon the wrong principle. If the pensioner is apparently legally married the commission have no power according to English law to require him to prove the legality of the marriage other than the fact of its existence. If they question its validity on the ground of incapacity of either party or for any other irregularity the onus should be upon the commission to establish that fact and to ask a man to go back twenty years and establish the death of a previous wife is to my mind absurd.

Legion as interpreted by the past president and heartily endorsed by the legion at the closing session of that convention. He said:
It was our distinct understanding, and, I am convinced, the understanding of all members of the committee, that the principle of merger between the tribunal and the pension board would be followed and, in fact, it was for the purpose of placing tribunal members on an equal status with the members of the old board that equal tenure of office for all was decided upon;-

I now turn to the matter of the appointments to the new commission, which took place at the end of September, 1933, effective, as provided by statute, on October the '1st, 1933. I must make it clear, and it will be admitted by the authorities, that no effort in any way, shape or form was made by the legion to influence these appointments. We relied implicitly on the understanding reached at the parliamentary committee, to the effect that, the principle of merger between the tribunal and the pension board would govern the appointments, and we relied upon the authorities to make the best selection from each body. We had let it be known that in our judgment the amount of work in sight would require the appointment of the maximum number provided for, namely, twelve commissioners.
It was with the utmost astonishment and I say frankly, dismay, that we learned from the press that of the eight members appointed to the new commission (the minimum provided for), five were of the old board of pension commissioners and its staff; one was a former commission counsel; another was a newcomer to pension administration; and one member and one only had been a member of the former pension tribunal, namely one of our dominion honorary presidents, General Sir Richard Turner, V.C. Not only had the principle of merger, agreed upon with the parliamentary committee, not been carried out, but of even greater significance to ex-service men, the new commission had been placed almost entirely under the domination of the old pension board'.
This action, coming immediately on top of the other disturbing happenings to which I have referred, brought about a state of mind throughout the entire legion and amongst ex-service men generally that I can only describe as chaotic. The soldier felt that here was proof of what he had already begun seriously to suspect, namely, that powerful influences were using all the means in their power to his detriment. The immediate reaction was one of intense resentment, accompanied by strong evidence of lack of confidence in legion officers, the first and perhaps natural conclusion being that these appointments would not have been made without the concurrence
[Mr. Gray.1
of legion officers. I am thankful that we were fully able to dispel this impression; but in the meantime the legion became seriously threatened with nation-wide disruption. Fuel was added to the flames by the announcement of the appointment of the chief reviewing officer, as provided under the act, the appointee being another member of the staff of the old pension board, making a total of seven out of nine. Storms of protest from coast to coast rolled in upon dominion headquarters. Explanations were of no avail, or at least could give little satisfaction. I, as your dominion president, sensing that the very existence of the legion was in grave jeopardy, after consultation with available dominion officers, and in accordance with a resolution passed' by dominion executive council in January, 1933, decided to announce the holding of a dominion convention, to take place early in 1934. British Columbia, to whom the next convention had been pledged, unselfishly relinquished its claim, in order that the convention might meet in Ottawa, the seat of government and it is to deal with these issues we are here to-day.

At this point let me say that upon the appointments being announced, feeling that it was my duty to make a public statement, I ventured the opinion that the appointments would not prove satisfactory to ex-service men, a statement which I thought mild and conservative, and' I asked that the new commission should be given a fair trial before being judged adversely. While we on this side of the house always have been kindly disposed towards the minister, and have appreciated his work with regard to ex-soldiers, at this time I cannot help but express my keen disappointment in the appointments that have been made. Their work became very unsatisfactory, and I am sure I am correct when I say that the first suggestion of an appeal court was made by the late Mr. Hume Cronyn, at one time a member of this house from the city of London. Those who took an interest in this work at that time will remember that the board had to try to make decisions not after a study of weeks, days, hours, or even minutes; the pressure of work was so great that they had to decide cases practically in seconds. They could not do the impossible.
Then came the tribunals. That legislation was drawn up originally by the soldiers themselves at a convention held in Regina, but it was not so presented to this house. It was presented to the house as a partisan measure, and hon. gentlemen tried to capitalize on it not only in the house but in the country as well. That change was adopted by the house. It was adopted also in the committee, but not without some objection, because I for one had grave misgivings as to its workability. We adopted it, however, because of the fact that it was what the soldiers wanted. It did not go as far as I thought it should
go, and when my hon. friend's leader was in power I had the distinction of being the only person to whose private resolution closure was applied. Closure was applied to a resolution that I brought in reversing the onus of proof. It never even got to a vote; closure was put on and it was sent to the committee. So far as I could judge, the personnel of the tribunals was satisfactory to the returned soldiers. Personally I was disappointed, and I think it was a mistake, that more of them were not reappointed, not because others could not do the work, but because at last we had found a tribunal in which the soldiers had confidence. I think all hon. members will agree that the machinery had become hopelessly clogged. A couple of years ago I made some remarks in this connection and I believe at that time in one court or another there were about 30,000 cases waiting to be heard. The clogging of that machinery led to an overhauling of it. I always thought the government made a mistake when the commission was appointed; I think all governments make mistakes when they place such matters outside their own power. Half were appointed by the returned soldiers and the other half by the staff of the department. It is a mistake for any government to put itself into the hands of a committee over which they have no control. When you put responsibility upon anybody you must also give him power; that goes without saying. The machinery was overloaded, and for the present we have another system of courts.
Whether we like it or not, I think in the last analysis we must admit that the government is responsible and that it must take the responsibility for the personnel appointed. Whether they have made a mistake or not I cannot say, nor do I think anybody else can; but I think it is only fair to these men that at least they should have reasonable time within which to prove their adaptability and their ability to handle matters placed before them. I have said before, the worst thing which could happen returned soldiers in this country is to have their case get into politics. If it were made a political question the country would be split in two, with half the people on one side and the other half on the other.
Returned soldiers can go only so far and get only such elements of justice as public opinion in Canada will support. I say to them to-night, as I have said to them before, that they should keep their demands within reasonable bounds of justice, because I am certain that parliament has always been willing to grant such demands. In that connection I want to refer to a letter that was written by Mr. Soammell, the secretary of the department, on January 10, 1934, giving figures with regard to the work done by the tribunals. I want to indicate from these figures that the tribunals certainly could not be charged with being unduly favourable to the ex-service men, and on the other hand it will be found that their judgment has been well upheld by the appeal court. Let me give the figures.
Out of a total number of 10,438 oases dealt with by the tribunals, 6,593 were decided unfavourably to the soldier and 3,845 favourably to the soldier. Of these 3,845 decisions favourable to the applicant, 899 were not appealed. That left 2,946 'as the total number of tribunal decisions favourable to the applicant appealed by commission counsel. Of these, 488 had not been heard by the appeal court on January 10, 1934. I deduct those, and it leaves 2,458 oases heard by the appeal court, and in 906 of these cases the tribunals' decisions were upheld; 342 oases were remitted for rehearing, and in the remainder of the eases the decisions were reversed.
Here is the summary: Tribunal cases decided in favour of the applicant, 3,845; appealed to but not heard by the appeal court, 488; leaving 3,357 cases, and of that 3,357, 342 cases were sent back for rehearing, leaving 3,015 cases actually disposed of by the appeal court or not appealed from. The net result of those 3,015 cases which the tribunal decided favourably to the applicant is that 899 cases were not appealed, and in 906 cases in which an appeal was made the tribunal's decision was upheld. So that in 1,805 out of 3,015 cases, or an average of over 60 per cent, the decisions of the tribunal in favour of the applicant stood. I think that those figures should be put on record in justice to the tribunal and for the benefit of those-there are not so many of them in the house-in the country who feel that the tribunals decided too favourably to the soldiers. In the first place they decided 6,500 out of 10,400 cases against the soldier, and of the 3,105 cases that they decided favourably to the soldier 1,805 were upheld by the appeal court or were not appealed from. So it seems to me that there is some justification for the feeling that it would have been advisable to appoint some of the tribunal to the new pension commission. Of course we are going to accept the suggestion of my hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario that the new men be given a chance to make good. But it is going to be somewhat difficult for
them, no doubt, on account of their lack of experience in dealing with cases in direct contact with the applicants throughout the country.
One thing more in regard to what my hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario has said. He said that the tribunal system worked badly because it was too much clogged. I have never felt that the tribunal system should be blamed for that, because there was one thing that clogged it, and that was an act of this parliament which provided that there should be an automatic reference to the tribunal of every case decided unfavourably to the soldier, with the result that the tribunal got piled up with cases put on their doorstep by statute. We amended the act a year ago and provided that those cases should not go from the board to the tribunal unless the applicant expressly asked for it, with the result that a different situation exists to-day. Both the tribunal and the pensions advocates, did remarkably well to clean up as many as 10,000 cases which were dealt with by the tribunal, in view of the immense accumulation of work ahead of them. They were new men with a lot to learn, but they did their work expeditiously and well, and they should not be blamed for the damming back of cases with which they were flooded. The new commission will not have that situation to meet, because the soldier himself must say whether or not he wants his case to be proceeded with further.
I do not know that I have anything to add except to pay a tribute, as I think tributes should be paid-and not too many have been paid-to the work of the tribunals which certainly laid the ground for confidence among the soldiers from the fact that they had an opportunity to meet in person the men who were going to decide their cases. I think that that did a lot to allay the discontent and dissatisfaction which existed when men simply made a report to a medical examiner, saw their papers sent away, and in two or three or four weeks the soldier got an adverse decision without a chance to tell his story. The tribunal system was in advance of the system of deciding cases without meeting the applicant face to face, and the present commission will continue this idea, which is germane and fundamental to any humane and satisfactory administration of pension matters, by travelling around the country hearing cases in the field.

This man died from aortic aneurysm, the result of specific infection. The initial infection, according to his military documents, was incurred prior to his enlistment, but the resulting condition was aggravated during his service, and as he had service in France, under section 12 of the Pension Act he received' during his lifetime pension for aggravation at the amount of his total disability.
He died in February, 1932, following which the relationship of his death to his military service was considered by the commissioners, and in accordance with an interpretation of section 12 of the Pension Act handed down by the Justice department, the commissioners ruled that the man's death had been caused by the aggravation during his service. The dependent widow was accordingly awarded pension.
In June, 1933, however, the pension appeal court gave a ruling regarding the interpretation of section 12, namely, that no pension could be awarded to the dependents of exsoldiers who had died from specific infection, whether incurred prior to enlistment and aggravated during service, or incurred during service, and accordingly the pensions of all widows and dependents in cases of death from preenlistment specific infection were discontinued. In this particular ease the discontinuance of pension was effective from October, 1933.
In view of this interpretation of section 12 of the Pension Act by the pension appeal court, the commissioners had no alternative but to take the action which was taken in this case, namely to discontinue this widow's pension.
I presume the action taken by the appeal court in that case was under the powers given to them by this house in section 65 of the act of last year, subsection (c), by which they have power in regard to "any question of interpretation of this act which may be referred by the crown or, by leave of the court, submitted by any applicant; and the procedure on such reference shall be as prescribed by the court."
I also recall that the royal commission of 1923, in regard to section 12, made a very strong and specific recommendation, that the discretion to award pensions should be exercised with regard to dependents, even where misconduct was on service. And this is a case, like many others, of pre-enlistment misconduct, widows being deprived of pension so many years after the war, notwithstanding that the royal commission recommended the exercise of discretion, and the Department of Justice having construed section 12 of the act as containing that discretion. This being so, it is unfortunate that the appeal court in their wisdom should have interpreted sec-

tion 12 as they have done, thereby bringing about the cessation of many pensions, without the pensioners concerned knowing the exact cause of such cessation.

The hon. member for South
Perth (Mr. Sanderson) spoke about the benefit of the doubt clause, and I am wondering whether hon. members have really touched the crux of the matter as it was put to me by the returned men's organization before I came to Ottawa. I think there is a great deal of merit in their claim. Subsection (a) of section 11 states:
Pensions shall be awarded to or in respect of members of the forces who have suffered

Unemployment and Farm Relief
disability in accordance with the rates set out in schedule A of this act, and in respect pf members of the forces who have died in accordance with the rates set out in schedule B of this act, when the injury or disease or aggravation thereof resulting in disability or death in respect of which the application for pension is made was attributable to or was incurred during such military service.
The word "incurred" is in clause (a), but when one comes to clause (c) hon. members will find 'that the word "incurred" has been left out. The returned men's organization which interviewed me maintained that the board of pension commissioners took no notice whatever of clause (a), but that they based their findings on clause (b), and if that is the case section 73, the benefit of the doubt clause, has no effect. That is evident, because in subsection (c) the word "attributable" is left out, the word "incurred" alone remaining, and a man has to prove hospitalization during the time he was in France or England before he is able to prove that the injury from which he is now suffering was incurred in service. At the time the act was drafted the words "attributable to" were put in so as to give a man the reasonable benefit of the doubt of injuries attributable to war service and from which he might be suffering to-day. I believe it is because this expression is left out of subsection (c) that there is a good deal of unrest and dissatisfaction from one end of the country to the other, especially on the part of those who have been turned down, due to the fact that they were not able to bring proof or to show in the records that they had incurred disability while serving either in France, in England, or with the forces.
I think these matters should be taken into consideration. If the minister is contemplating any changes in the act he would do well to look into the wording of subsection (a) and note that while in that subsection the words "attributable to" appear, they are left out of subsection (c), and there is just the word "incurred"; so that in dealing with section 73 the board has been looking only at subsection (c) and ignoring subsection (a). That is the crux of all the trouble and the dissatisfaction of many returned men who find themselves suffering from ailments attributable to war service.
While the cases in which the question of marriage is involved have been discussed, I have before me a complaint which is entirely different but which I . believe should be mentioned. My understanding is that the act did not come into force until October 1 of last year. In the changes made last year there
was provision under which any children born after May 1 would not be granted a pension or could not be registered. I have had several complaints from my own constituency about children bom in the month of June. Apparently the board were acting ahead of time; at least they were acting before the law had been made operative by official notice. I think from the investigations I have made that we were perhaps a little to hasty last year when we enacted that legislation regarding children born after June 1, 1933. Many men who served at the front are still comparatively young men, and when that clause was put in we were, in a way, telling them that children they had in future would not be registered with the board of pension commissioners, nor would they receive any pension on their account. But cases that happened in June of last year should have been registered and should have received the small pension, at least until such time as the governor in council made the proclamation in October, 1938. I am sorry to have taken up the time of the committee, Mr. Chairman, but these matters are very important.
